front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Open switch

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Closed switch

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Cell

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Battery (two or more cells connected in series)

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Diode

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Fixed resistor

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Variable resistor

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Filament lamp

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Fuse

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Voltmeter

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Ammeter

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Thermistor

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Light-dependent resistor (LDR)

front: Name this circuit symbol
back: Light-emitting diode (LED)

front: Define balanced forces
back: A resultant force of zero on an object

front: Define braking distance. What can affect it?
back: The distance a vehicle travels under the braking force. This can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions as well as the condition of the vehicle.

front: Which forces require contact between objects, and which don't?
back:
Contact forces: friction, air-resistance (air is an object) normal force
Non-contact forces: weight, electrostatic force, magnetic force

front: Define elastic limit
back:
The force beyond which an object will no longer deform elastically, and will
instead deform plastically. It will not return to its original shape.

front: Define friction
back: A resistive contact force that acts to opposes the direction of movement

front: Define hooke's law
back:
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied to it, up
to the limit of proportionality.

front: Define human reaction time
back:
The time it takes for the brain to react to a stimulus. Typical human
reaction times are in the range of 0.2-0.9 seconds.

front: Define Newton
back: The unit of force.

front: State Newton's first law (2 cases)
back:
When the resultant force is zero:
  • A stationary object stays stationary
  • A moving object continues at constant velocity (same speed and direction)

front: Define Newton's second law
back: An object’s acceleration is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it, and inversely proportional to the object’s mass: F=ma

front: Define resultant force
back:
The single force that can replace all the individual forces acting on an
object, and have the same effect.

front: Define terminal velocity
back:
The maximum velocity an object can reach when falling through a fluid. It
occurs when the resistive forces equal the object’s weight.

front: Define thinking distance
back:
The distance a vehicle travels during the driver’s reaction time. This
reaction time may be affected by tiredness, drugs or alcohol.

front: Define velocity and its unit.
back: A vector quantity that is a measure of the rate of change of displacement. It is the speed in a given direction. Unit is m/s

front: Define weight
back: The force of matter due to gravity. It is equal to the product of mass and gravitational field strength, and so varies depending on your location in the universe.

front: Explain what is meant by a scalar quantity. Give 2 examples
back:
A scalar quantity is a quantity with a magnitude, but no direction.
E.g. distance, speed, time, mass, energy..

front: Explain what is meant by a vector quantity. Give 2 examples
back:
A vector quantity has both a magnitude and a direction.
E.g. Force, velocity, displacement, momentum, moment...

front:
Which property of a distance-time graph
can be used to calculate speed?
back: Gradient (or Slope)

front: For these distance–time (d–t) graphs, which is at rest, constant speed, and accelerating?
back:
• A: constant speed (straight diagonal line)
  • B: at rest / stationary (flat horizontal line)
  • C: accelerating (curve getting steeper)

front:
What is meant by acceleration?
Give its unit.
back: A vector quantity that is the change in velocity per unit of time. Unit is m/s2

front:
Which property of a velocity-time graph can be used
to calculate acceleration?
back: Gradient (slope)

front:
Which property of a velocity-time graph can be used
to calculate distance travelled?
back: Area under the graph

front: For these velocity–time (v–t) graphs, which is constant speed, accelerating, and decelerating?
back:
• A: constant velocity (flat horizontal line)
  • B: constant acceleration (sloping upward)
  • C: constant deceleration (sloping downward)

front: Name two types of forces that always oppose motion
back:
1. Friction
2. Air Resistance (Drag)

front: Which type of force holds planets around the Sun?
back: Gravitational Force

front: Which type of force holds electrons around nucleus?
back: Electrostatic Force

front: State three ways a force can affect an object
back:
- It can change the shape of the object (extension/compression)
- It can change the speed of the object
- It can change the direction the object is moving

front:
What factors that affect the stopping distance
of a car?
back:
- Reaction time
- Weather conditions
- Initial speed
- Driver’s conditions
- Road Conditions
- Mass of the car
- Tire Conditions

front:
State two factors that affect the air
resistance acting on a falling object
back:
- Surface Area
- Speed

front: Compare elastic and plastic behaviour
back:
• Elastic behaviour: object returns to its original shape when the force is removed
  • Plastic behaviour: object is permanently deformed when the force is removed

front: Define alternating current
back: Current flow consisting of charges that continually change direction.

front: Define ampere (amp)
back: The unit of current

front: Define circuit breaker
back:
A safety device that cuts off the power supply if a surge of current passes
through it. Circuit breakers can be reset and are quicker acting than fuses.

front: Define Coulomb
back: The unit of charge.

front: Define diode
back:
A component that only allows current to flow through in the forward direction. They
have very large resistances in the reverse direction.

front: Define direct current
back: Current flow consisting of charges flowing in a single direction only.

front: Define earth wire (incl. colour)
back: The green and yellow wire connected to metal casings of appliances, that prevents an appliance from becoming live.

front: Define electric current
back:
The rate of flow of electrical charge. Its value is the same at any position in
a single closed loop. In metals, the charges that flow are electrons.

front: Define filament lamp
back:
A light emitting component consisting of an enclosed metal filament. Its
resistance increases as the filament’s temperature increases.

front: What is a fuse, how does it work, and which wire is it on?
back:
• Safety device containing a thin metal wire
  • If current exceeds its rating (e.g. 5 A), the wire melts and breaks the circuit
  • Always connected in the live wire

front: Define insulator
back: A material that doesn’t allow electrical charge to flow.

front: Define light dependent resistor (LDR)
back:
A light sensitive component whose resistance decreases
as its temperature increases.

front: Describe a light-emitting diode (LED) (3 points)
back:
• Allows current to flow in one direction only
  • Emits light when current flows through it
  • Requires a minimum voltage before it lights up (useful for indicating current)

front: Define live wire (incl. colour)
back: The brown wire that carries the current from the supply to the appliance.

front: Define mains electricity
back: An a.c supply, which in the UK has a frequency of 50Hz a value of 230V.

front: Define neutral wire (incl. colour)
back: The blue wire that completes the circuit in a mains power supply

front: Define ohmic conductor
back:
A conductor whose current flow is directly proportional to the potential
difference (voltage) across it, when held at a constant temperature.

front: Define ohm
back: The unit of resistance.

front: Define Ohm's law
back:
The current flowing through an Ohmic conductor at constant temperature is
directly proportional to the potential difference (voltage) across it.

front: State the rules for voltage and current in a parallel circuit
back:
• Voltage (p.d.): the same across every branch
  • Current: total current = sum of currents in each branch

front: Define potential difference
back: The energy that is transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit. It is often also called a voltage

front: Define resistance
back: A measure of the opposition to current flow

front: What happens to total resistance in parallel?
back: The total resistance is less than the lowest individual resistance.

front: How do you calculate total resistance of resistors in series?
back: The total resistance is equal to the sum of the resistances of the individual resistors.

front: What is a series circuit?
back:
Components are connected in a single line, so the same current passes through each
component.

front: Define thermistor
back:
A temperature dependent component, whose resistance increases as its
temperature decreases.

front: Define volt
back: The unit of potential difference (voltage). One volt is equal to one joule per coulomb.

front: Define watt
back: The unit of power.

front: Describe the structure of an atom, including particle charges
back:
• Small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing protons (+1) and neutrons (0)
  • Surrounded by electrons (−1) orbiting in shells at different distances

front: This symbol represents a cell. Which side is the positive (+) terminal?
back: Left side (the longer, thinner line is always positive +; the shorter, thicker line is negative −)

front: How is a thermistor affected by changes in temperature?
back:
As temperature increases, its resistance
decreases

front: Voltage is also known as ….
back: Potential difference

front: Compare current and voltage in series vs parallel circuits
back:
• Series: current is the same everywhere; total voltage = sum of component voltages
  • Parallel: voltage is the same across each branch; total current = sum of branch currents

front: What is a voltmeter and where must it be connected in a circuit?
back: A device that is connected in parallel with a component to measure the potential difference (voltage) across it.

front: State what a Volt is equivalent to in other units.
back: Joule per Coulomb

front:
What is an ammeter and where must it
be connected in a circuit?
back:
An ammeter measures current. It is
placed in series with the component it is
required to measured.

front: What are the two things needed for a continuous current to flow?
back: A potential difference (voltage) and a closed circuit

front: How does changing resistance affect current (at constant voltage)? (2 points)
back:
• Current is inversely proportional to resistance — higher resistance gives a smaller current
  • Higher resistance makes it harder for electrons to flow through the circuit

front:
How can you use a variable resistor to
increase the current in a series circuit?
back:
You set the variable resistor to have a
lower resistance, this should increase
the current.

front: Explain the I–V relationship for a filament lamp (3 points)
back:
• As current rises, the filament gets hotter
  • Metal ions vibrate more → more frequent electron collisions → resistance increases
  • Non-ohmic: current is not directly proportional to voltage (I–V graph curves and flattens)

front: Which electrical component does this I–V graph represent?
back: Diode (only conducts current in one direction once threshold voltage is reached)

front: Why does a resistor heat up when current flows through it? (2 points)
back:
• Flowing electrons collide with metal ions in the resistor’s lattice
  • Energy is transferred from electrical/kinetic energy to thermal energy in the surroundings

front:
How do low resistance wires reduce
unwanted energy transfers?
back:
A smaller resistance will mean there are
fewer collisions, therefore less energy
will be wasted through heating.

front: Give 1 advantage and 2 disadvantages of the electrical heating effect
back:
• Advantage: useful in heating appliances (kettles, toasters, electric heaters)
  • Disadvantages: wastes energy (lowers efficiency); overheating can damage components or cause fire

front: Which voltage–time graph shows a.c. and which shows d.c.?
back:
• A: alternating current (a.c.) — continuously reverses direction
  • B: direct current (d.c.) — flows in one direction only

front:
What type of current do batteries and
cells supply?
back: Direct current.

front: How does an earth wire keep a metal-cased appliance safe? (3 points)
back:
• Connected to the metal casing, providing a low-resistance path to ground
  • If the live wire touches the casing, a large current flows to earth
  • This melts the fuse / trips the circuit breaker, cutting off the supply

front: Why must a fuse or switch be connected in the live wire? (2 points)
back:
• The live wire carries the high voltage (230 V) from the supply
  • Breaking the live wire isolates the appliance so it cannot remain live and cause an electric shock

front:
Explain what is meant by
double insulation.
back:
When casing of an appliance is made out of
plastic, it is said to be double insulated since
plastic is an insulator and does not let electricity
pass through.

front: Which wire is not needed in a double-insulated appliance, and why?
back:
• Earth wire is not required
  • The outer casing is made of plastic (an electrical insulator), so it cannot become live

front:
Circuit breakers can be used instead of fuses.
Give 2 advantages of circuit breakers over
fuses
back:
More sensitive
Easier to reset
Does not need to be replaced.

front: Define Doppler effect
back: The change in a wave’s observed wavelength and frequency when there is relative motion between its source and an observer.

front: Describe gamma rays: nature, penetration, uses and hazards (4 points)
back:
• High-energy electromagnetic wave emitted from an unstable nucleus
  • Very high penetration — needs several centimetres of lead or thick concrete to absorb
  • Uses: sterilising food/medical kit, detecting & treating cancer
  • Hazard: ionising — can cause cell damage and DNA mutations

front: Define Hertz (Hz)
back: The unit of frequency.

front: What is infrared radiation?
back:
A type of radiation that all objects emit and absorb. The hotter an object
is, the greater the infrared radiation it emits in a given time.

front: Define law of reflection
back:
The angle of incidence must always equal the angle of reflection when a
wave reflects.

front: What is a ray diagram?
back:
• A diagram showing the path of light / waves (e.g. at a mirror or glass boundary)
  • Drawn as straight lines with arrows showing the direction of wave travel

front: Define reflection
back: The bouncing back of a wave at a boundary

front: Define refractive index
back:
The ratio of the speed of the wave in a vacuum to the speed of the wave
in a given medium.

front: Define sound waves
back:
The longitudinal waves responsible for sound. They require a medium to
travel through and are transmitted by the vibrations of the medium’s particles.

front: Define wave velocity
back:
The velocity at which energy is transferred through the medium. It is equal to
the product of the wave’s wavelength and frequency.

front: Define wave
back:
A process of energy transfer through oscillations, without matter being transferred
with it.

front: Define wavefront
back:
An imaginary surface representing points of a wave that are at the same point in
their cycle.

front: Define wavelength
back:
The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the adjacent wave
(ie. peak to peak or trough to trough).

front:
Waves transfer ______ and ______
without transferring _______.
back: Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.

front: Define frequency and give its units.
back:
● The number of waves passing through a point per second.
● Hz (hertz)

front: Define amplitude.
back:
● The maximum displacement of the wave from its equilibrium position.

● The distance between the centre of the wave and a peak

front:
What is meant by the period of the
wave?
back:
The length of time it takes for one full
wave to pass through a point .

front:
What is a longitudinal wave? Give some
examples.
back:
● Vibrations/oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer(wave)

● Examples include sound waves and earthquakes (seismic waves)

front:
What is a transverse wave? Give some
examples.
back:
● A wave with oscillations that are perpendicular (90 degrees) to the direction of energy transfer.

● Examples include electromagnetic waves, water waves

front:
At what speed does an electromagnetic
wave travel in a vacuum?
back: 3 x10<sup>8</sup> m/s

front: Give 4 properties shared by all electromagnetic waves
back:
• All are transverse waves
  • All travel at the same speed in a vacuum (speed of light, 3 × 108 m/s)
  • All transfer energy (and information)
  • All can be reflected and refracted

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum has the longest wavelength?
back: Radio waves

front:
Order the electromagnetic spectrum from
the highest frequency to the lowest
frequency.
back:
Gamma rays, x-rays, ultraviolet, visible
light, infrared, microwaves and radio
waves

front:
What are the colours of the visible light
spectrum?
back:
Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue,
Violet.

front: Which colour has the highest frequency?
back: Violet

front: Which colour has the lowest frequency?
back: Red

front: Which colour has the lowest wavelength?
back: Violet

front: Which colour has the highest wavelength?
back: Red

front: What are the uses of radio waves?
back:
● For communication through radio
● Used for satellite transmissions

front: What are microwaves used for?
back:
● Cooking in microwaves ovens
● Communications
● Satellites

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used in cooking, thermal
imaging and television remote controls?
back: Infrared

front: Give examples of uses for visible light
back:
● Allows us to see (used for vision)
● Photography
● Optical Fibres
(endoscope, communication)

front:
What part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used for security marking
and in fluorescent lamps?
back: Ultraviolet

front: What are some uses of x-rays?
back:
● Scanners at airports
● Medical x-ray machines

front:
What are the disadvantages of
microwaves?
back:
They can cause heating of internal
tissues in the body

front:
Which part of the electromagnetic
spectrum is used in TV remotes and can
also cause skin burns?
back: Infrared

front:
Does the danger that is associated with
electromagnetic waves increase with
frequency or with wavelength?
back: With frequency

front:
What are the dangers of excessive
exposure to ultraviolet?
back:
You could damage your eyes and the
cells on the surface of your skin. This
could lead to skin cancer or eye
conditions.

front:
What is the normal (in terms of reflection
and refraction)?
back:
A vertical imaginary line which is
perpendicular to the boundary.

front: What happens to light when it refracts at a boundary? (3 points)
back:
• Light changes speed and (at an angle) direction
  • Entering a more optically dense medium: slows down and bends towards the normal
  • Entering a less optically dense medium: speeds up and bends away from the normal

front: What is the critical angle?
back: The angle of incidence in the denser medium that produces an angle of refraction of 90° (light refracts along the boundary).

front: What are the 2 conditions for total internal reflection (TIR)?
back:
• Light must travel from a more optically dense medium towards a less optically dense medium (e.g. glass → air)
  • The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle (i > c)
  • All the light is reflected back inside the denser medium

front: State two uses of total internal reflection
back:
Any two of:
- Endoscopes
- Periscopes
- Optical Fibres
- Cat Eye Reflectors
- Shining of Diamonds

front: How does sonar / echo-sounding measure distance? (3 steps)
back:
• Emit a pulse of sound/ultrasound; it reflects off a boundary and the echo is detected
  • Measure total time t and calculate total distance = speed × time
  • Divide by 2 (because the wave travelled there and back)

front: Which letter represents the wavelength?
back: D (distance from one crest to the next crest — one complete wave cycle)

front: Which letter represents the amplitude?
back: A (maximum displacement from the central equilibrium rest position to a crest or trough)

front: Define chemical energy
back: A store of energy found in things such as batteries, fuels and food.

front: Define closed system
back: A system that does not interact with the wider unidervse; nothing enters or leaves

front: Define conduction
back: The transfer of heat energy through the vibrations of particles in a medium.

front: Define conservation of energy
back: The law that energy can be transferred, stored or dissipated but never created or destroyed.

front: Define convection
back: The transfer of heat energy through convection currents in a fluid.

front: Define elastic potential energy
back: The store of energy that stretched or compressed objects contain.

front: Define electrostatic potential energy
back:
The store of energy due to the relative position of a charge
in an electric field.

front: Define gravitational potential energy (GPE)
back:
• Energy stored by an object because of its position in a gravitational field (height)
  • Depends on mass, gravitational field strength (g) and height (GPE = mgh)

front: Define heat transfer
back:
The transfer of thermal energy from a hotter region to a cooler region,
through conduction, convection or radiation.

front: Define joule
back:
The unit used for energy. Equal to the work done when a force of one Newton acts
over a distance of one metre.

front: Define kinetic energy
back: The store of energy that all moving matter has.

front: Define lubrication
back:
The application of a lubricant (such as oil) to reduce the friction that acts
between surfaces. This may improve the efficiency of a system.

front: Define magnetic energy
back: The potential energy of a magnet.

front: Define nuclear energy
back: The store of energy found in the nuclei of atoms.

front: Define radiation
back:
The transfer of energy, without the transfer of matter. No medium is needed for
radiation to occur.

front: Define sankey diagram
back: A diagram used to show the energy transfers of a system

front: Define surface temperature
back:
The temperature of a body is determined by the rate at which they
absorb and emit radiation.

front: Define thermal energy
back:
The higher
the temperature, the greater an object's thermal energy store.

front: Define useful energy transfer
back:
The transfer of energy by a system, to directly serve the purpose
of the system.

front: Define work done
back:
• Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance
  • Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force (W = Fd)

front: State the 8 main stores of energy
back:
• Kinetic
  • Gravitational
  • Thermal
  • Chemical
  • Elastic
  • Magnetic
  • Electrostatic
  • Nuclear

front:
What are the four main transfer types between
energy stores?
back:
- Mechanically (or forces)
- Electrically
- By heating
- By radiation (light and sound)

front:
What changes are involved when a ball
(initially stationary) rolls down a hill?
back:
● GPE turns into KE as it rolls downwards

● The speed will increase as the vertical height decreases

front: What is wasted energy? Give an example.
back:
• Energy transferred to a store that is not useful for the device’s intended purpose (usually dissipated as thermal energy)
  • Example: sound or heat lost to the air from a kettle

front: Explain why a kettle’s heating element is placed at the bottom (4 points)
back:
• Water at the bottom is heated, expands and becomes less dense
  • Warm, less dense water rises
  • Cooler, denser water sinks to replace it
  • Sets up a convection current that heats all the water

front:
How does the thickness of a building’s walls
affect the rate of cooling?
back:
The thicker the building walls are the further heat
has to travel to escape, hence as you increase
the thickness you decrease the rate of cooling.

front:
How does the thermal conductivity of a building’s
walls affect the rate of cooling?
back:
The higher the thermal conductivity the easier it is for
heat to escape, so a higher rate of cooling.

front: Give 3 ways to reduce unwanted heat transfer in a home
back:
• Loft / cavity wall insulation — traps air to reduce conduction & convection
  • Double glazing — trapped air/vacuum gap reduces conduction
  • Curtains / shiny foil — reduce heat loss by convection and infrared radiation

front:
What is the relationship between work
done on an object and energy
transferred to the object?
back:
Work done = energy transferred
W = ΔE

front: Define power in two ways
back:
- The rate at which energy is transferred.

- Work done(energy transferred) per unit of time

front: What is 1 watt equivalent to in terms of other units?
back: 1 Watt = 1 joule per second (J/s).

front: Define absolute zero
back:
The lowest possible temperature: −273°C or 0K. At this temperature the particles have no
kinetic energy and so are completely stationary.

front: Define density
back: The mass per unit volume of an object.

front: Define kelvin
back:
The SI unit of temperature, based on an absolute temperature scale; it is proportional to the
average kinetic energy of the molecules.

front: Define Pascals
back:
The unit of pressure, equal to a force of one Newton acting perpendicular to an
area of one metre squared.

front: What is gas pressure?
back:
The perpendicular force per unit area acting on the surfaces of a
container as a result of the gas particles colliding with it. It acts equally in all directions.

front: Define pressure
back: The force acting perpendicular to a surface, per unit area.

front: Define temperature in terms of particles
back:
• A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance
  • Higher temperature → particles have higher average kinetic energy and move faster

front: How can Pascals be expressed in other units?
back:
1 Pa = 1 Nm2
(1 newton per square metre)

front:
In which direction does pressure act in liquids or
gases?
back: It acts in all directions equally

front:
How do you convert between degree
Celsius and Kelvin?
back:
• °C → K: add 273 (T(K) = θ(°C) + 273)
  • K → °C: subtract 273 (θ(°C) = T(K) − 273)
  • Absolute zero: 0 K = −273 °C

front: Explain how a gas exerts pressure on its container walls (3 points)
back:
• Gas particles move rapidly in random directions
  • They collide with the container walls, exerting a force at right angles to the wall
  • Total force per unit area = pressure

front:
How does changing the temperature of a
gas affect the velocity of the particles?
back:
The higher the temperature, the more
kinetic energy the particles have and
therefore the faster the average velocity
of the particles.

front: Explain why heating a gas (at constant volume) increases its pressure (3 points)
back:
• Particles gain average kinetic energy and move faster
  • They collide with the walls more frequently and harder (greater force)
  • Greater force per unit area → pressure increases

front: How does changing the volume of a gas affect its pressure (at constant temperature)?
back:
• Pressure and volume are inversely proportional (p1V1 = p2V2)
  • Smaller volume (compressed): particles collide more frequently → pressure increases
  • Larger volume (expanded): fewer collisions per second → pressure decreases

front:
State 2 assumptions you should make while
using P<sub>1</sub> x V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub> x V<sub>2</sub>
back:
- Fixed mass(number of molecules)
- Fixed Temperature

front: Why does compressing air in a bicycle pump raise its temperature? (3 points)
back:
• Pressing the piston does work on the gas as volume decreases
  • Transfers energy to the gas particles → their average kinetic energy increases
  • Higher average kinetic energy means a higher temperature

front:
Give an example of how unwanted
energy transfer while heating can be
reduced.
back:
Through using insulation, which prevents
energy being transferred to the
surroundings.

front: How does a simple d.c. electric motor rotate? (3 points)
back:
• A current-carrying coil sits in a magnetic field
  • Current flows in opposite directions on opposite sides of the coil
  • The two sides experience forces in opposite directions (motor effect), causing rotation

front: Define electromagnet
back:
A solenoid with an iron core. The magnetism of an electromagnet can
be switched on and off, and the strength changed, through varying the current in the
solenoid.

front: Define the generator effect (electromagnetic induction) (2 points)
back:
• Relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field (cutting field lines) induces a voltage
  • An induced current flows if the conductor is part of a complete circuit

front: Define an induced magnet (3 points)
back:
• A magnetic material that becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field
  • Loses its magnetism quickly when removed from the field
  • Always produces an attractive force

front: Define magnetic field lines
back: Lines that show the strength and direction of a magnetic field; they never cross.

front: What are magnetically hard materials? Give examples.
back:
Materials that are permanently
magnetised. Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel (or steel, an iron alloy)

front: What are magnetically soft materials? Give an example.
back:
• Easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise (temporary magnets)
  • Example: soft iron (used in electromagnet cores and transformers)

front:
How do the different poles of the
magnet interact?
back: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract each other

front: What is a magnetic field?
back:
A region surrounding a magnet where
other magnets will experience a force.

front:
Which direction do the field lines in a
magnetic field point?
back: From north to south.

front:
Does a high concentration of field lines
mean the field is strong or weak?
back: Strong

front: How do you produce a uniform magnetic field?
back:
• Place opposite poles (N and S) of two flat magnets facing each other
  • Field lines between them are straight, parallel and equally spaced

front: How do you use a plotting compass to map a magnetic field? (4 steps)
back:
• Place the magnet on paper and put a plotting compass near one pole
  • Mark a dot at the tip of the needle, then move the tail of the needle to that dot
  • Repeat to trace a line from North pole to South pole
  • Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow from N → S

front:
Use your hand to show Fleming’s Left
Hand rule, stating which finger represent
field quantity.
back:
● Force (thumb)
● Magnetic field (index finger)
● Current (second finger)
● FBI

front:
How can we increase the magnitude of the
force acting on a current-carrying wire inside
a magnetic field?
back:
● Increase the size of the current
● Increase the strength of magnetic field (Use stronger magnet)

front: What is the motor effect and what causes it?
back:
• A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force
  • Caused by the interaction between the wire’s magnetic field and the external magnetic field

front: Explain how a loudspeaker works (4 steps)
back:
• Alternating current (a.c.) flows through a coil attached to a cone inside a magnetic field
  • The motor effect produces a force on the coil/cone
  • Because the current reverses, the force reverses direction → the cone vibrates
  • Vibrating cone creates sound waves (pressure variations) in the air

front: How are electric motors kept rotating?
back:
A commutator is used. This switches the
current direction every half turn, which
ensures that the coil keeps spinning.

front:
What factors affect the size of an
induced voltage?
back:
● The number of turns on the coil of wire
● How strong the magnetic field is
● How fast you move the magnet

front: How does an alternator generate alternating current (a.c.)? (3 points)
back:
• A coil rotates inside a magnetic field, cutting field lines to induce a voltage
  • Each side moves up then down every half turn, so the induced current reverses direction
  • Connected via slip rings → outputs a.c.

front:
What is the shape of the magnetic field
created around a straight wire when a
current is running through?
back:
• Concentric circles centred on the wire (closer together near the wire where field is stronger)
  • Direction found with the Right-Hand Grip Rule (thumb = conventional current + → −)

front:
What rule can you use to determine the
direction of a current or magnetic field
around a wire?
back:
The right hand rule
  • Grip a wire with the thumb in the direction of current (conventional)
  • The fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.

front: Define activity
back: The rate at which an unstable nucleus decays, and so the rate at which radiation is released.

front: Define alpha particle
back:
A helium nucleus (2 neutrons and 2 protons).

They are highly ionising, but can be stopped by a few centimetres of air.

front: Define background radiation
back: Radiation that is found in small quantities all around

front: Define beta particle
back:
A high speed electron that a nucleus emits when a neutron converts into a
proton. They are ionising but can be stopped by a thin sheet of aluminium.

front: Define chain reaction
back:
The process of neutrons released by a fission reaction, being absorbed by
another unstable, large nuclei, and inducing further fission.

front: Define fission products
back:
Fission produces two smaller nuclei, two or three neutrons and gamma
rays. These products are released with kinetic energy.

front: Define Geiger-Muller tube
back: A device used to detect ionising radiation.

front: Define half-life (2 equivalent definitions)
back:
• Time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay
  • OR: time taken for the activity / count rate of a sample to halve
  • Constant for a given isotope (different for different isotopes)

front: Define ionising radiation
back: Radiation that can cause atoms to lose or gain electrons, leading to cell mutations, damage cells and tissues, and lead to cancers.

front: Define irradiation
back:
The process of an object being exposed to nuclear radiation. The object doesn’t
become radioactive.

front: Define nuclear fission
back:
• The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two smaller daughter nuclei
  • Releases energy and 2–3 neutrons (used in nuclear power stations)

front: Define PET scanner
back:
A medical imaging device that uses radioactive tracers and detectors to form
internal body images.

front: Define photographic film
back:
A material that reacts to ionising radiation, allowing an image to be
formed.

front: Define radioactive decay
back:
The random process involving unstable nuclei emitting radiation to
become more stable.

front: Define shielding
back: A barrier used to prevent radioactive daughter products leaving a nuclear reactor.

front: Define uranium-235
back:
The radioactive isotope used in nuclear reactors. It is often referred to as
U-235.

front:
What is meant by an “isotope” of an
element?
back:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element
with same atomic(proton) number and
different mass(neutron) number.

front:
What is the relative masses of a proton,
neutron and electron?
back:
● Proton: 1
● Neutron: 1
● Electron: roughly 1/2000

front: Why is an atom neutral?
back:
An atom contains the same number of protons as
electrons and neutrons have no charge.

front:
Which types of radiation are emitted from
unstable nuclei?
back:
● Alpha Particles
● β– (beta minus) Particles
● Gamma rays
● Neutron radiation

front: Give 3 sources of background radiation
back:
• Rocks & soil (especially radon gas)
  • Cosmic rays from space
  • Medical uses (X-rays, radiotherapy) · food & drink · nuclear fallout

front:
State two pieces of equipment which can be
used to detect radiation.
back:
● Geiger-Müller (GM) Detector
● Photographic Film

front:
Order the types of ionising radiations
starting with the least ionising to most
ionising
back: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

front:
Order the types of ionising radiation,
starting with the most penetrating first.
back: Gamma → Beta → Alpha

front:
When alpha decay occurs, what
happens to the atomic number and the
mass number of the atom?
back:
- The atomic number decreases by 2

- The mass number decreases by 4 (a new element is made)

front:
What effect does releasing gamma
radiation have on the mass number and
atomic number of an atom?
back: No effect

front: How does beta minus (β<sup>−</sup>) decay change mass number and atomic number?
back:
• A neutron turns into a proton + electron (β− particle emitted)
  • Mass number: stays the same
  • Atomic number: increases by 1

front:
What happens in the atom to cause
gamma rays to be released?
back:
When the nucleus decays some of the
nuclei rearranges itself so there is an excess
energy. This may lead to it releasing this
energy in the form of gamma rays.

front:
How does the activity of a radioactive
source decrease over a period of time?
back:
It decreases by a constant ratio over constant
time periods. For example, every 10 minutes a
sample of a radioactive substance may
quarter its activity

front: What is the unit for activity?
back: Becquerel (Bq)

front:
Can you predict when a nucleus will
decay?
back: No, the process is a random process.

front: Give 3 examples of uses of radioactivity.
back:
- Household fire alarms (smoke)
- Irradiating food
- Sterilisation of equipment
- Tracing and gauging thicknesses of materials
- Diagnosis and treatment of cancer

front: Explain how a smoke alarm uses alpha radiation (4 steps)
back:
• An alpha source inside the detector ionises air between two plates
  • Ions allow a steady small current to flow
  • Smoke absorbs alpha particles → air is no longer ionised → current drops
  • Drop in current triggers the alarm

front: How is radiation used in medicine?
back:
● To sterilise equipment: Gamma radiation can kill bacteria cells

● To help treat cancer, as it as it can be used to kill cancer cells

front: How is beta radiation used to control material thickness? (3 points)
back:
• Beta source on one side of the sheet, detector on the other
  • High count rate → sheet is too thin (rollers move slightly apart)
  • Low count rate → sheet is too thick (rollers press closer together)

front: Give 4 safety precautions when handling radioactive sources
back:
• Handle with long tongs (never touch directly; keep distance)
  • Keep exposure time as short as possible
  • Store in lead-lined containers
  • Wear protective clothing / use lead shielding and point away from people

front:
Does a long half life or a short half life
make a source more dangerous?
back:
If it has a long half life then it would
remain highly radioactive for longer
therefore making it more dangerous.

front: State the difference between contamination and irradiation
back:
• Contamination: unwanted radioactive atoms get onto or inside an object/body (keeps emitting radiation until removed/decayed)
  • Irradiation: an object is exposed to radiation from an external source (stops as soon as you move away or shield it)

front: How is a radioactive tracer used in medicine? (3 points)
back:
• Gamma-emitting isotope (short half-life) is injected, swallowed or inhaled
  • Gamma rays pass out of the body and are detected by an external gamma camera
  • Tracks blood flow / organ function to produce an image

front: Explain the process of fission of U-235.
back:
The U-235 absorbs a neutron which makes it
unstable, this causes it to split into two
daughter nuclei and release two or more
neutrons, as well as releasing energy.

front: What is the job of a moderator?
back:
It slows down the neutrons until they are
travelling at a speed slow enough for
them to be absorbed.

front:
How are control rods used to ensure a
controlled reaction?
back:
● They are raised or lowered so that they absorb fewer or greater neutrons
● The number of neutrons that they absorb determines how many reactions can take place

front: What is nuclear fusion?
back:
When two small nuclei fuse together to
form a larger nuclei. This process also
releases energy.

front: Where does fusion occur everyday?
back:
In the sun - stars use fusion as their
energy source

front: Why is nuclear fusion difficult to use as an energy source on Earth? (2 points)
back:
• Both nuclei are positively charged and strongly repel electrostatically
  • Requires extremely high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion (hard and expensive to sustain)

front: Define artificial satellites
back:
Man-made satellites that have been sent into space for purposes such
as satellite imaging and communications.

front: Define comets
back:
Objects consisting of rock, dust and ice that travel in the universe at high speeds.
When they approach the sun they vaporise and produce a trail.

front: Define galaxy
back: A system containing billions of stars.

front: Define main sequence star
back:
The stable state of all stars. The gravitational forces pulling the star
together, and the pressure pushing outwards, are balanced.

front: Define Milky Way galaxy
back: The galaxy in which our solar system is located.

front: Define natural satellites
back: The moons that orbit planets.

front: Define orbital radius
back:
The radius of a body’s orbit. For a stable orbit, a change in its orbital radius
is required for the body to undergo a speed change.

front: Define orbital speed
back:
A measure of how fast an object orbits. It is directly proportional to the orbital
radius and inversely proportional to the orbital period.

front: Define orbital period
back: The time it takes for an object in orbit to complete one full cycle.

front: Define protostar
back:
The first stage all stars go through after forming from a nebula. In this stage the
star becomes hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse.

front: Define red giant star
back:
When their hydrogen is used up and larger nuclei are produced by fusion,
stars of a similar magnitude to the Sun will expand to form a red giant.

front: Define universe
back: A large system of billions of galaxies.

front: Define white dwarf
back:
When the fusion reactions in stars of a similar magnitude to the sun come to
an end, the star will contract under gravity and cool down to form a white dwarf.

front: Why does your weight change on different planets? (2 points)
back:
• Weight = mass × g (your mass stays constant)
  • Gravitational field strength (g) varies with a planet’s mass and radius

front: What objects make up our Solar System? (4–5 items)
back:
• The Sun (our star)
  • 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune)
  • Moons (natural satellites)
  • Dwarf planets, asteroids and comets

front: Describe the orbits of planets, moons and comets (3 points)
back:
• Planets: nearly circular orbits around the Sun
  • Moons & artificial satellites: nearly circular orbits around planets
  • Comets: highly elliptical orbits around the Sun

front:
Which force is makes astronomical objects
follow orbits?
back:
Gravitational force pulls the objects
causing them to follow orbits around
massive objects.

front:
Stars can be classified according to colour.
Order the given colours of stars from coldest to
hottest:
● Yellow
● Blue
● Red
● White
● Orange
back:
Coldest → Hottest
Red → Orange → Yellow → White → Blue

front: Which stage is the Sun currently in?
back: Main sequence

front: What is a nebula?
back: A cloud of gas and dust in space

front: How does a nebula become a main sequence star? (3 steps)
back:
• Gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) together → forms a protostar
  • Particles speed up and collide harder → core becomes hotter and denser
  • Core gets hot enough for nuclear fusion (H → He) to begin → main sequence star

front: Why is a main sequence star stable? (3 points)
back:
• Nuclear fusion fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing huge energy
  • Creates an outward radiation / thermal pressure
  • Outward pressure balances inward gravitational pull (forces in equilibrium)

front:
What happens when a star transitions to
the red giant stage?
back:
● Once all of the hydrogen fuel has been used up, the star begins to fuse helium and other larger nuclei

● This causes the star to expand and become a red giant

front:
How does a star become a white dwarf
from a red giant?
back:
● Once all reactions have taken place, the star’s gravity pulls in all of its mass, making a small, dense white dwarf

● This will cool down to form a black dwarf

front:
What stages occur for the evolution of
stars that have a mass which is larger
than the sun?
back:
- Nebula
- Main sequence star
- Red supergiant star
- Supernova
- Black hole/ neutron star

front: What is a supernova and what remains afterwards? (2 points)
back:
• The violent explosion of a red supergiant at the end of its life (scatters heavy elements into space)
  • Leaves behind a dense neutron star — or a black hole if the core is massive enough

front: Which electrical component does this I–V graph show?
back: Metal filament lamp (non-ohmic — resistance increases as the filament heats up)

front: Which electrical component does this I–V graph show?
back: Wire / fixed resistor at constant temperature (ohmic conductor — I is directly proportional to V)

front: What do the different straight-line slopes on this I–V graph show?
back:
• Fixed resistors at constant temperature (each is ohmic: straight line through origin)
  • Steeper gradient = lower resistance; shallower gradient = higher resistance

front: Explain the shape of this diode I–V graph in forward and reverse bias (2 points)
back:
• Reverse bias (negative V): very high resistance → virtually zero current flows
  • Forward bias (positive V): once voltage exceeds the threshold voltage (~0.6 V), resistance drops sharply and current rises steeply

front: State the 8 main forces
back:
• Weight (gravity)
  • Static electric force
  • Magnetic force
  • Thrust
  • Friction
  • Air/water resistance (drag)
  • Upthrust
  • Normal (contact) force

front: Core practical: how do you accurately investigate the motion of a toy car or falling ball? (3 points)
back:
• Measure distance with a metre ruler and time with a stopwatch (or light gates to eliminate human reaction-time error)
  • Repeat readings at each distance and calculate a mean (excluding anomalies)
  • Calculate average speed using v = d ÷ t and plot a distance–time graph

front: Core practical: how do you investigate force vs extension for a spring, metal wire and rubber band? (3 points)
back:
• Measure original length with a ruler at eye level (avoids parallax error), add slotted masses, and calculate extension = new length − original length
  • Spring: straight line through origin up to elastic limit (obeys Hooke’s law)
  • Rubber band: curved graph (does not obey Hooke’s law); loading & unloading curves differ

front: Why is current conserved at a junction in a circuit?
back:
• Electric charge is conserved (electrons are neither created nor destroyed)
  • Therefore total current entering a junction = total current leaving the junction

front: Why is the voltage the same across components connected in parallel?
back:
• Each parallel branch connects directly across the same two points of the power supply
  • Every coulomb of charge transfers the same energy across each branch → voltage is identical across every branch

front: State the 3 rules for calculating resistance, current and voltage for two resistors in series
back:
• Total resistance: Rtotal = R1 + R2
  • Current: I = Vsupply ÷ Rtotal (same through both resistors)
  • Individual voltages: V1 = I R1 and V2 = I R2 (and V1 + V2 = Vsupply)

front: What 2 boundary behaviours are shared by ALL waves (light, sound, water, EM)?
back:
• Reflection: waves bounce off a boundary with angle of incidence = angle of reflection
  • Refraction: waves change speed (and direction if entering at an angle) when crossing into a different medium/depth

front: Core practical: how do you trace a refracted ray through a glass block or prism? (3 steps)
back:
• Draw around the block on paper and shine a narrow beam from a ray box
  • Mark incident and emergent rays with pencil crosses, remove block, and join entry & exit points
  • Draw a normal (at 90°) where the ray meets the boundary and measure i and r from the normal with a protractor

front: Core practical: how do you find the refractive index (n) of glass accurately using a graph?
back:
• Measure pairs of angle of incidence (i) and angle of refraction (r) for 5+ different angles
  • Plot sin i (y-axis) against sin r (x-axis) → straight line through the origin
  • Gradient of the line = refractive index n (n = sin i ÷ sin r)

front: Core practical: give a classic experiment to demonstrate conduction, convection and radiation
back:
• Conduction: pins waxed along rods of different metals heated at one end (copper drops pins first)
  • Convection: potassium manganate(VII) crystal heated at bottom of water beaker shows purple rising/sinking loop
  • Radiation: compare cooling of matt black vs shiny silver cans of hot water (matt black cools fastest)

front: How does conservation of energy link GPE, KE and work done?
back:
Assuming negligible air resistance / friction:
  • Falling object: GPE lost = KE gained (mgh = ½mv2)
  • Force moving an object: work done (W = Fd) = energy transferred (gain in GPE or KE)

front: Core practical: how do you measure the density of regular solids, irregular solids and liquids?
back:
Always measure mass on a top-pan balance, then use ρ = m ÷ V:
  • Regular solid: measure l, w, h with ruler/callipers (V = l × w × h)
  • Irregular solid: find volume by water displacement (measuring cylinder or eureka can)
  • Liquid: mass = (cylinder + liquid) − empty cylinder; read volume at bottom of meniscus

front: How does pressure act at a point inside a liquid or gas at rest?
back:
• Acts equally in all directions at any given depth
  • Increases with depth (h) and fluid density (ρ) (p = ρgh)

front: Core practical: how do you investigate the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation? (3 points)
back:
• Measure the background count rate first (with no source) and subtract it from every reading
  • Place absorbers in turn between source and GM tube: paper, thin aluminium (few mm), thick lead
  • Count drop shows: α stopped by paper; β stopped by aluminium; γ greatly reduced by thick lead

front: How do you balance a nuclear decay equation?
back:
• Total mass number (top) must be equal on both sides
  • Total atomic number / charge (bottom) must be equal on both sides
  • Key symbols: α = 42He · β− = 0−1e · neutron = 10n

front: How do you find half-life from a decay curve or activity data? (3 points)
back:
• Subtract background count first (if given)
  • From a graph: read the time for activity to halve (e.g. 800 → 400 Bq); check a second halving (400 → 200 Bq) and average
  • Calculation: count how many halvings occur (A0 → A0/2 → A0/4…) and multiply by one half-life

front: Name 3 nuclear processes that can act as sources of energy
back:
• Nuclear fission (used in nuclear power stations)
  • Nuclear fusion (powers the Sun and stars)
  • Radioactive decay (e.g. powers deep-space probes & geothermal heat)

front: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion
back:
• Fission: splitting a large unstable nucleus (e.g. U-235) into smaller daughter nuclei + neutrons (used in nuclear reactors)
  • Fusion: joining two small light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen → helium) at extreme temperature & pressure (powers stars)

front: Why does gravitational field strength (g) differ on different planets and moons?
back:
• g depends on the mass (larger mass → larger g) and radius of the planet/moon
  • Earth: ~10 N/kg · Moon: ~1.6 N/kg (much smaller mass) · Jupiter: much larger than Earth

front: How is a star’s colour related to its surface temperature?
back:
• Hotter stars appear blue / white (emit more short-wavelength light)
  • Cooler stars appear orange / red
  • Order from hottest to coolest: blue → white → yellow → orange → red

front: In the investigating motion practical, why are light gates better than a handheld stopwatch?
back:
• Light gates eliminate human reaction-time error (~0.2 s)
  • Measure very short time intervals with much higher resolution and accuracy

front: If a 4 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in series across a 20 V supply, find the current and each resistor’s voltage
back:
• Total resistance: R = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω
  • Current: I = V ÷ R = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A (same in both)
  • Voltages: V1 = 2 × 4 = 8 V · V2 = 2 × 6 = 12 V (check: 8 + 12 = 20 V)

front: What changes — and what stays the same — when a wave refracts into a slower medium?
back:
• Speed decreases and wavelength decreases
  • Frequency stays constant (set only by the wave source)

front: In the refraction practical, where must you measure angles i and r from?
back: • Always measure angles i and r from the normal (the dashed line drawn at 90° to the surface), never from the glass edge

front: A ball falls from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how do you find its speed just before hitting the ground from its starting height h?
back:
• Set GPE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv2
  • Mass m cancels → v = √(2gh) (speed doesn’t depend on mass!)

front: Why does water spurt further out of a hole near the bottom of a tall tank than from a hole near the top?
back:
• Liquid pressure increases with depth (p = ρgh) because of the greater weight of liquid above
  • Pressure acts equally in all directions, pushing water sideways out of the lower hole with greater force

front: In the radiation penetration practical, why must you subtract the background count rate and take repeat readings?
back:
• Subtract background: ensures you only measure radiation from the source, not natural background
  • Repeat & average: radioactive decay is random, so averaging gives a more accurate count rate

front: Where does the energy released in fission, fusion and radioactive decay come from?
back: • Transferred from the nuclear energy store of atomic nuclei into kinetic energy of the products and thermal / radiation energy

front: Why is an astronaut’s weight smaller on the Moon than on Earth, even though their mass is unchanged?
back:
• Mass is the amount of matter (stays constant everywhere)
  • The Moon has much smaller mass → smaller gravitational field strength g (~1.6 vs ~10 N/kg), so W = mg is smaller

front: Which star has a higher surface temperature: a blue-white star or a red giant? Explain briefly.
back:
• A blue-white star has a much higher surface temperature
  • Hotter stars emit more high-frequency / short-wavelength blue light; cooler stars peak in longer-wavelength red light
